questions.stem: Who introduced the HOOK technique for data warehousing?
options: Bill Inmon
Ralph Kimball
Andrew Foad
Dan Linstedt
Edgar Codd
questions.explanation: HOOK is described as a new term introduced by Andrew Foad, a hybrid methodology that borrows from Data Vault and Kimball.

questions.stem: What is the single structure that HOOK uses instead of the many table types of Data Vault and Kimball?
options: A Hub
A Bag
A Satellite
A Fact table
A Bridge
questions.explanation: Where Data Vault and Kimball have Hubs, Links, Satellites, Dimensions and Facts, HOOK has one structure called a Bag that wraps an existing warehouse table.

questions.stem: In HOOK, what does a Bag expose from the table it wraps?
options: Surrogate keys generated by the warehouse
Row-level security policies
Aggregated measures for reporting
Business Keys aligned to Business Concepts in the Enterprise Data Model
Compression settings for the storage layer
questions.explanation: A Bag wraps an existing data warehouse table and exposes Business Keys that align to Business Concepts defined in the Enterprise Data Model (EDM).

questions.stem: How are HOOK Bags typically implemented?
options: As materialised tables reloaded nightly
As stored procedures
As views defined over existing data warehouse tables
As separate physical databases
As flat files in object storage
questions.explanation: Bags are typically implemented as views over existing warehouse tables, which is why they can be dropped and recreated without reloading data.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of qualifying each HOOK Key with a Key Set?
options: To compress the key for faster storage
To encrypt the business key at rest
To record when the key was last refreshed
To decide which Bag the key belongs to
To identify the set of values the Business Key belongs to so that joins do not produce unintended matches
questions.explanation: A Key Set formally identifies the set of values a Business Key belongs to, so that only keys with the identical Key Set match when Bags are joined.

questions.stem: In the loan example from I Am Datapedia!, why is there no risk of customer C123 from CRM colliding with C123 from CoreBank?
options: The two systems are never loaded into the same warehouse
Hook values include Key Sets, so the two keys are distinct values
CoreBank renumbers its customers on ingestion
The join is done on customer name instead of ID
The warehouse rejects duplicate IDs at load time
questions.explanation: Because Hook values such as 'CRM.CUS.ID|C123' and 'CBNK.CUS.ID|C456' carry their Key Set, keys from different systems cannot accidentally match.

questions.stem: How does HOOK differ from Data Vault regarding modelling before ingestion?
options: HOOK requires a full logical model before any data is loaded
HOOK requires more upfront modelling than Data Vault
HOOK does not require upfront modelling before ingesting data
HOOK forbids ingesting data until every Business Concept is approved
HOOK and Data Vault take exactly the same approach
questions.explanation: Unlike Data Vault, HOOK does not require upfront modelling; ingestion and business modelling run in separate sprints, and Bags are built later in Alignment sprints.

questions.stem: Which statement about HOOK is described as a common misconception?
options: That HOOK is a data warehouse modelling approach
That HOOK can be layered over existing architecture
That Bags can be implemented as views
That HOOK Keys must carry a Key Set
That HOOK borrows features from Kimball
questions.explanation: HOOK is not a modelling approach; it is an approach to organising warehouse objects around business language, and it does not prescribe any specific modelling method.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a Hook column used in the LoanApproval join example from I Am Datapedia!?
options: HK_Customer
HK_Officer
HK_Date
HK_Branch
HK_Loan
questions.explanation: The example joins Frame_LoanApproval to Customer, Officer and Date frames on HK_Customer, HK_Officer and HK_Date, with HK_Loan identifying the loan; there is no HK_Branch.

questions.stem: Why is the HOOK approach described as extremely agile?
options: Because it stores all data in memory
Because it eliminates the need for business keys
Because it replaces SQL with a graphical query language
Because it requires a single central modelling team
Because Bags as views can be dropped and recreated without reloading data or consuming resources
questions.explanation: Since Bags can be represented as views, they can be dropped and recreated freely, letting HOOK be layered over existing architecture with little or no impact.
